passages.title: Learning in the School Garden
passages.text:
Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

activities.instruction: Read passage P1 and choose the best answer.

items.question: Where is the garden?
items.explanation: The first sentence locates the garden behind the library.

items.question: Who chose the plants?
items.explanation: The teacher helped with planning, but the pupils chose the plants.

items.question: Why is there a narrow path?

options.C: To avoid stepping on young plants

items.explanation: The path provides a route between the beds without damaging plants.

items.question: What problem did the open buckets cause?
items.explanation: The passage explicitly describes spilled water.

items.question: How did the bottles help?
items.explanation: Small holes allowed slow watering near the roots.

items.question: What did the pupils do when leaves turned yellow?

options.B: They sought help and compared notes

items.explanation: They asked the teacher and used their records; no diagnosis is supplied.

items.question: Which lesson best fits the passage?

options.A: A large garden always gives more learning
options.B: Flowers are more useful than vegetables
options.C: Cooperation and careful use of resources matter
options.D: Children should use tools without checking them

items.explanation: The final paragraph states what made the class proud.

items.question: How was the teacher involved in the bottle idea?

items.question: What does each group record?
items.modelAnswer: Each group records the weather, plant growth and the work it has done.

items.question: Why were the children proud after the harvest?

activities.instruction: Write a short summary of P1 in your own words. Include the main activity, an improvement and the central lesson. No official word limit is asserted.
activities.modelAnswer: A Class Six group cares for a school garden with guidance from its teacher. The pupils reduce wasted water by using checked bottles and keep records to understand changes in the plants. They share their first vegetables with the school kitchen. The project teaches them cooperation and responsible use of resources.
assessment: Includes gardening as a shared class project
Mentions an evidence-based example of careful resource use or recording
Retains the lesson of cooperation and responsibility
Uses connected, accurate sentences rather than copying the entire passage
unacceptableInferences: A specific disease caused the yellow leaves
The teacher chose all the plants

endings.C: the class shared vegetables with the kitchen.
endings.D: Rupa proposed slow watering through small holes.

activities.instruction: Arrange these sentences into a connected account. Underlined connectors are not required; use the time clues.

sentences.A: After collecting them, the class washed and sorted the containers.
sentences.B: With the planting finished, a group put the pots on a safe shelf.
sentences.C: First, the teacher asked everyone to collect suitable used containers.
sentences.D: A week later, the first shoots appeared in the pots on the shelf.
sentences.E: Before filling the clean containers, the teacher checked them for damage.
sentences.F: After filling them, the children planted seeds in the soil.
sentences.G: Seeing the shoots, they began measuring their height each morning.
sentences.H: Once the check was complete, the children filled the containers with soil.

activities.explanation: The chain is collecting → washing → checking → filling → planting → placing → shoots appearing → measuring. The explicit references establish that order.

activities.instruction: Complete this story in a coherent way: On the way home, Mina found a small bag on a bench. She looked around, but no one was nearby. Then she noticed a school badge on the bag ...
activities.modelAnswer: Mina recognised the badge of a nearby school. She did not open the bag or take it home. Instead, she went to the school office and told the teacher on duty where she had found it. The teacher kept the bag safely and contacted the class teachers. Soon a worried pupil arrived with his mother. Before handing it over, the teacher asked them to describe the bag and its contents. Their description matched. The boy thanked Mina because his exercise books were inside. Mina was glad that she had asked a responsible adult for help. She returned home and told her family what had happened.
assessment: Continues the given opening without contradiction
Has connected events and a plausible ending
Uses consistent narrative tense and clear references
Avoids encouraging unsafe contact with strangers
activities.note: Original model completion. Other coherent, safe endings are acceptable; this is not a memorisation-only answer.

activities.instruction: Write a paragraph about working together at school. Explain one shared task, how responsibilities can be divided and why listening matters.
activities.modelAnswer: Working together at school helps us learn from one another. Last month, our class organised a small reading corner. We first discussed what we needed and listened to different suggestions. Some pupils collected suitable books, while others cleaned the shelf with help from a teacher. Another group made labels so that readers could find stories easily. We divided the work according to our abilities, not according to who was the loudest. When two friends disagreed about the labels, they explained their ideas and chose a clear design together. We also made a simple rule about returning books after reading. The corner was small, but everyone had a chance to contribute. I learned that teamwork requires patience, fairness and responsibility. A shared task becomes easier when we respect others and ask for help when necessary.
assessment: Addresses a shared school task with relevant details
Presents connected ideas as a paragraph
Uses age-appropriate vocabulary, grammar and punctuation

activities.instruction: Write a short dialogue between two classmates planning a reading corner. Include a suggestion, a question, a polite response and an agreed plan.

modelAnswer.speaker: Asha
modelAnswer.line: Could we make a reading corner in our classroom?

modelAnswer.speaker: Rafi
modelAnswer.line: That sounds useful. Where could we put the books?

modelAnswer.speaker: Asha
modelAnswer.line: There is a spare shelf beside the window. We should ask our teacher first.

modelAnswer.speaker: Rafi
modelAnswer.line: Good idea. How will we collect suitable books?

modelAnswer.speaker: Asha
modelAnswer.line: We can invite classmates to lend books they are willing to share.

modelAnswer.speaker: Rafi
modelAnswer.line: Shall we label them so that none gets lost?

modelAnswer.speaker: Asha
modelAnswer.line: Yes. We can keep a notebook showing who borrows each book.

modelAnswer.speaker: Rafi
modelAnswer.line: I can help make the labels. Would you speak to the teacher with me?

modelAnswer.speaker: Asha
modelAnswer.line: Certainly. Let us ask after class today.

modelAnswer.speaker: Rafi
modelAnswer.line: Agreed. Then we can discuss the plan with everyone.

assessment: Speakers respond meaningfully to one another
Includes suggestion, question, polite response and agreement
Maintains a clear purpose and natural sequence
Uses readable speaker labels and appropriate language
